changes.new: ### AGC: a separate bound for each output unit Two output units can have equal gradient norms and very different weight norms. For example, let the rows of a linear weight matrix be $(3,4)$ and $(0.03,0.04)$, with the same gradient $(0.3,0.4)$ on each row. Both gradients have norm $0.5$, but the weight norms are $5$ and $0.05$. An SGD step of size $0.1$ changes the first row by 1% of its norm and the second by 100%. A global threshold cannot distinguish those two relative changes. Brock, De, Smith and Simonyan motivate adaptive gradient clipping in [§4 of the NFNet paper](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v139/brock21a.html): > However in practice, we clip gradients based on the unit-wise ratios of > gradient norms to parameter norms, which we found to perform better > empirically than taking layer-wise norm ratios. This is an original English passage, reproduced under CC BY 4.0. For a weight matrix $W\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, row $W_i$ contains the incoming weights of output unit $i$. Write $G_i$ for the corresponding gradient row and define $$ \begin{aligned} s_i&=\max(\|W_i\|_2,\varepsilon_W),\\ b_i&=\lambda s_i,\\ \widetilde G_i&= \begin{cases} G_i\,b_i/\|G_i\|_2,&\|G_i\|_2>b_i,\\ G_i,&\text{otherwise}. \end{cases} \end{aligned} $$ The zero gradient uses the second branch. Each unit has its own bound $b_i$. In a convolution, the unit contains all input-channel and spatial weights of one output filter. A norm over the entire layer would merge those units. For the two rows above, choose $\lambda=0.2$. Their bounds are $1$ and $0.01$. The first gradient remains $(0.3,0.4)$; the second is multiplied by $0.01/0.5=0.02$ and becomes $(0.006,0.008)$. The relative SGD changes are now $0.01$ and $0.02$. For a unit whose weight norm exceeds $\varepsilon_W$, plain SGD without momentum satisfies $\|\Delta W_i\|/\|W_i\|\le\eta\lambda$. The clipped matrix no longer points in the same direction as the original matrix when all its entries are concatenated. AGC preserves each nonzero row's direction, while allowing different rows to shrink by different factors. Global norm clipping instead multiplies every row by the same factor; with a global threshold of $0.5$, both example rows would shrink by $1/\sqrt2$. ```python import torch def agc_linear_rows(W, G, *, clipping=.2, weight_floor=1e-3): # Dense [out_features, in_features] matrices; finite CPU example. # This is not a wrapper for arbitrary tensor layouts or sparse gradients. assert W.ndim == 2 and W.shape == G.shape assert clipping > 0 and weight_floor > 0 assert torch.isfinite(W).all() and torch.isfinite(G).all() weight_norm = W.norm(dim=1, keepdim=True).clamp_min(weight_floor) gradient_norm = G.norm(dim=1, keepdim=True) bound = clipping * weight_norm clipped = G * (bound / gradient_norm.clamp_min(1e-6)) return torch.where(gradient_norm > bound, clipped, G) W = torch.tensor([[3., 4.], [.03, .04]], dtype=torch.float64) G = torch.tensor([[.3, .4], [.3, .4]], dtype=torch.float64) clipped = agc_linear_rows(W, G) torch.testing.assert_close(clipped, torch.tensor( [[.3, .4], [.006, .008]], dtype=W.dtype)) relative_step = (.1 * clipped).norm(dim=1) / W.norm(dim=1) torch.testing.assert_close(relative_step, torch.tensor( [.01, .02], dtype=W.dtype)) # The weight floor lets a zero-initialized unit receive an update. zero_weights = torch.zeros_like(W) zero_case = agc_linear_rows(zero_weights, G) torch.testing.assert_close(zero_case.norm(dim=1), torch.full( (2,), .0002, dtype=W.dtype)) assert torch.equal(agc_linear_rows(W, torch.zeros_like(G)), torch.zeros_like(G)) print(clipped, relative_step) ``` The floor $\varepsilon_W=10^{-3}$ is the paper's default, not a replacement for choosing $\lambda$. Without a floor, a zero-initialized unit would receive a zero bound and could remain frozen. Near zero, the bound is relative to the floor rather than to the actual weight norm. The authors' [reference implementation, commit f5de0ede](https://github.com/google-deepmind/deepmind-research/blob/f5de0ede8430809180254ee957abf36ed62579ef/nfnets/optim.py#L446-L499) uses linear weights in input–output order and convolution weights in HWIO order. Its reduction axes therefore differ from the row-wise PyTorch example. Scalars and vectors also have a separate convention. Copying the same axis numbers into an OI/OIHW implementation would clip different units. The implementation applies AGC before SGD's momentum and weight decay. Those later operations, and Adam's moment normalization, are outside the plain-SGD relative-step bound derived above. ![[00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/gradient-clipping-2026-10-29/nfnet-agc-ablation.png|Original NFNet Figure 2: batch sizes and AGC thresholds]] *Andy Brock, Soham De, Samuel L. Smith and Karen Simonyan, [Figure 2, ICML 2021, PMLR 139:1059–1071, PDF p. 4](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v139/brock21a/brock21a.pdf#page=4), CC BY 4.0. Both original panels and the complete caption are retained. Only surrounding page text was cropped; labels and curves are unchanged.* Panel (a) compares ImageNet accuracy at different batch sizes, using the best tested clipping threshold for each batch size. It is not a comparison at one universal $\lambda$. Solid and dashed curves distinguish ResNet-50 and ResNet-200. Panel (b) varies $\lambda$ for ResNet-50; larger batches require stronger clipping in this experiment. Section 4.1 also excludes the final classifier from AGC after an ablation. These are NF-ResNet experiments with Nesterov SGD, not evidence that the same threshold or layer exclusions improve every Transformer. ### AutoClip: choose the threshold from raw gradient history A fixed clipping threshold is expressed in the units of the loss gradient. Multiplying every loss by ten multiplies its gradients by ten. The same numerical threshold then clips a different fraction of batches. AutoClip chooses a percentile of observed gradient norms instead of a fixed magnitude. The percentile $p$ remains a hyperparameter. Let $n_t=\|g_t\|_2$ be the norm before clipping. At update $t$, append this raw norm to the history, calculate its $p$-th percentile, then clip: $$ \begin{aligned} H_t&=(n_1,\ldots,n_t),\\ \tau_t&=Q_p(H_t),\\ \widetilde g_t&= g_t\min(1,\tau_t/n_t)\qquad(n_t>0). \end{aligned} $$ A zero gradient stays zero. The current norm participates in its own threshold; the first finite gradient is therefore unchanged in the ideal formula. The [authors' PyTorch implementation](https://github.com/pseeth/autoclip/blob/dfb622c3caca9dc0ecc8bf0afeb773e190256d6e/autoclip.py) uses this order and NumPy's percentile convention. For raw norms $10,2,4,100$, choose $p=50$ and linear interpolation between ordered observations: | Update | Raw norm | Sorted history | Median threshold | Norm sent to optimizer | |---:|---:|---|---:|---:| | 1 | 10 | 10 | 10 | 10 | | 2 | 2 | 2, 10 | 6 | 2 | | 3 | 4 | 2, 4, 10 | 4 | 4 | | 4 | 100 | 2, 4, 10, 100 | 7 | 7 | At the fourth update, the two middle observations are 4 and 10, giving $(4+10)/2=7$. Keeping only the clipped norms would produce a different history and change later thresholds. A 90th-percentile rule and a 10th-percentile rule are also very different policies: the latter clips far more gradients. ```python import numpy as np import torch def autoclip_vector(gradient, history, *, percentile=50.): if not 0 <= percentile <= 100: raise ValueError("percentile must be in [0, 100]") norm = torch.linalg.vector_norm(gradient).item() if not np.isfinite(norm): raise ValueError("do not put a nonfinite gradient into history") history.append(norm) # Raw norm, including this update. threshold = float(np.percentile(history, percentile, method="linear")) factor = 1. if norm == 0 else min(1., threshold / norm) return gradient * factor, threshold history, thresholds, sent = [], [], [] for raw in [10., 2., 4., 100.]: gradient = torch.tensor([.6 * raw, .8 * raw], dtype=torch.float64) clipped, threshold = autoclip_vector(gradient, history) thresholds.append(threshold) sent.append(clipped.norm().item()) np.testing.assert_allclose(history, [10., 2., 4., 100.]) np.testing.assert_allclose(thresholds, [10., 6., 4., 7.]) np.testing.assert_allclose(sent, [10., 2., 4., 7.]) print("raw:", history, "thresholds:", thresholds, "sent:", sent) ``` This finite-vector example isolates Algorithm 1. A training loop measures the norm over all selected parameter gradients after accumulation and, when used, AMP unscaling. It applies clipping before the optimizer updates its moments. The history and its configuration must be saved to resume the same procedure. A skipped nonfinite step should not append an infinity to the percentile history. At $p=100$, the threshold is the largest norm seen so far, including the current norm, so clipping does nothing in the ideal formula. At $p=0$, the threshold is the smallest observed norm; one zero in that history can make all subsequent clipped gradients zero. Neither endpoint is a general-purpose default. The original paper reports successful $p=1$ and $p=10$ settings on speech separation, rather than a universal 90th-percentile recipe. Multiplying every finite gradient in a fixed history by the same positive constant multiplies both $n_t$ and $\tau_t$ by that constant. Thus the clipping factors remain equal. This does not prove an identical training trajectory: SGD's updates still scale, Adam has $\varepsilon$, and a changed trajectory can generate different future gradients. A rolling window or an approximate quantile can reduce the cost of retaining and processing the growing history, but defines a different history estimator. ![[00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/gradient-clipping-2026-10-29/autoclip-mi.gif|Original AutoClip animation: parameter steps, training loss and gradient norms]] *Prem Seetharaman, Gordon Wichern, Bryan Pardo and Jonathan Le Roux, [original mask-inference animation and explanation](https://github.com/pseeth/autoclip/blob/dfb622c3caca9dc0ecc8bf0afeb773e190256d6e/README.md#training-dynamics), [MIT License](/licenses/autoclip-dfb622c3-MIT.txt). The complete 40-frame GIF is unchanged. This is the authors' speech-separation experiment, not a Bookvar training run.* The original README explains the panels: > Training dynamics of a smaller mask inference network (2 BLSTM layers with > 300 hidden units) with mask-inference loss and whitened k-means loss, with > and without AutoClip. The top left figure shows the norm of the step size > taken on the model parameters. The top right figure shows the training > loss over time, showing that AutoClip leads to better optimization. The > bottom figures show the relationship between gradient norm and a measure > of smoothness along the training trajectory. Statistics were recorded > every 20 iterations during training. With AutoClip, we observe a stronger > correlation (r-value of .86), compared to without (r-value of .62). All > gradients to the right of the dashed black line in the bottom right plot > are clipped. We show the location of the AutoClip threshold at the end > of training. The threshold changes during training. The source paragraph accompanies two animations; the one reproduced here uses mask-inference loss. The upper-left axis measures actual parameter displacement, not the raw norm used to select the threshold. The dotted line in the lower-right panel marks the final threshold; it should not be read as one fixed value for the entire run. The smoother observed Adam steps do not turn gradient clipping into a mathematical bound on Adam's step size. ## Смешанная точность
